How the major features of Chola power were connected

The Cholas are remembered for administrative institutions, agricultural prosperity, military expansion, monumental temples and bronze sculpture. These were different achievements, but several of them were closely connected.

The Kaveri delta formed the agricultural heartland of the kingdom. Irrigation through river channels, canals, tanks and wells helped farmers cultivate the land, particularly for rice production.

Agricultural production provided an important base for land revenue. The Chola government collected revenue, while village assemblies and nadu institutions also performed administrative responsibilities.

These resources helped sustain the monarchy and its wider activities. Royal and private donations also supported temples, where land endowments contributed to the maintenance of religious personnel and specialised craftspeople.

Alongside this land-based foundation, the Chola rulers exercised military power. Rajaraja I expanded and consolidated the kingdom, while Rajendra I carried its military reach towards the Ganga valley and overseas, including the 1025 CE naval expedition against Srivijaya.

Five distinctions that explain the system

1. Ur and sabha served different village contexts

The ur was associated with ordinary peasant settlements, while the sabha administered Brahmana land-grant settlements. The nadu comprised a larger group of villages, and the nagaram was associated with merchants in towns.

2. Land revenue and compulsory labour were different obligations

Kadamai referred to land revenue, while vetti referred to compulsory labour. Both were connected with the obligations imposed under Chola rule, but they were not the same form of contribution.

3. Natural water channels and constructed tanks performed different roles

The Kaveri's branches carried flowing water and deposited fertile soil. Constructed irrigation tanks stored collected water, while sluice gates and channels helped regulate its distribution.

4. Rajaraja I and Rajendra I had distinct major achievements

Rajaraja I was associated with administrative consolidation and the Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur, completed around 1010 CE.

Rajendra I was associated with the Ganga expedition, the 1025 CE naval expedition against Srivijaya and the temple at Gangaikondacholapuram, completed around 1035 CE.

5. Temple architecture and bronze sculpture were different artistic achievements

Chola temple architecture is represented by large stone structures in the Dravida tradition. Chola bronze sculpture is represented by cast metal images, especially Nataraja, made using techniques such as lost-wax casting.

Prelims focus

  • Ur, sabha, nadu and nagaram must be distinguished by their institutional roles.
  • Kadamai means land revenue; vetti means compulsory labour.
  • Kaveri delta agriculture depended on fertile soil and organised water management.
  • Rajaraja I is associated with Brihadisvara at Thanjavur; Rajendra I with Gangaikondacholapuram.
  • Rajendra I launched the major Srivijaya naval expedition in 1025 CE.
  • Chola bronzes are especially associated with lost-wax casting and Nataraja imagery.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7 History, Chapter 2, New Kings and Kingdoms, pp. 18, 22-27; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, pp. 81-85, and Chapter 7, Indian Bronze Sculpture, pp. 107-108; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Great Living Chola Temples, Brief Synthesis, consulted 18 November 2026; Hermann Kulke, The Naval Expeditions of the Cholas in the Context of Asian History, Chapter 1 summary, Cambridge Core, consulted 18 November 2026.]

title: Understanding the Connections Between Chola Administration, Irrigation, Naval Power and Temples
